He denied any recent new medication. His oral lesion was swabbed for mpox, and he was tested for chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and HIV. He was treated empirically with tecovirimat. panels.figure_caption: (a) Right-hand and (b) left-hand lesions of patient A upon presentation. The patient had similar umbilicated lesions on his entire body.
in_text_mentions: Patient A is a 41-year-old man with uncontrolled HIV, who presented to the ED with a 3-week history of worsening left-hand lesion (Figure 1b) that was soon followed by numerous scattered lesions on the trunk, face, right hand (Figure 1a), and perineal and scrotal skin. Additionally, raised red patches spread over the neck, trunk, and upper extremities. The patient was treated with pain control medications, antihistamines, and topical creams. A day later, painless papules appeared on the trunk and upper extremities.

in_text_mentions: Vital signs were as follows: The patient was alert. Respiratory rate was 16 breaths/min, body temperature was 38.4°C, pulse rate was 114 beats/min, blood pressure was 116/66 mmHg, and SpO2 was 100% on room air. His face was flushed, and mild pharyngeal erythema was present. Cervical lymphadenopathy was present without tenderness. There were no abnormal chest or abdominal findings. The patient presented with firm papules accompanied by central pustules on the anterior neck and thighs. Similar pustular papules were also observed on both hands (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: e seventh day: a pustule on the left lateral region of the neck and an erythematous papule on the left costal grill. On the eleventh day, all the lesions in the gluteal region and neck were erythematous-pustular, and some pustules were umbilicated. In addition, the patient mentioned that the lesions in the gluteal region were painful (Figure 2). Most lesions were crusted and painless on the fourteenth day. A papule appeared near the gluteal cleft (Figure 3). On the eighteenth day, several crusts fell off. On the twenty-first day all the scabs fell off and the patient was discharged (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Real patient clinical photograph of the dorsum of both hands showing tense, monomorphic pustules at a uniform stage of evolution with surrounding hyperpigmentation and edema. The article title identifies this as the first Clade Ib Mpox case in Kinshasa, and the caption describes classic mpox pustular lesions asymmetrically distributed on the extremities. Disease attribution and findings are directly supported. [raw subtype: Clade Ib] b: Real patient clinical photograph of both palms showing high-density asymmetrical pustules with confluence into pseudobullous lesions, a classic palmar mpox manifestation. Attribution to Clade Ib mpox is supported by the disease-specific article title together with the captioned palmar pustular eruption. [raw subtype: Clade Ib] c: Real patient clinical photograph of the dorsum of the foot showing isolated pustules all at the same stage of evolution, consistent with the synchronous monomorphic mpox eruption...
panels.attribution_text: Kasongo-Mulenda et al. Clade Ib Mpox in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): Clinical and Virological Report of the First Case in Kinshasa, the Capital City.. Viruses 2025. doi:10.3390/v17101327. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Hands, palms, and back and sole lesion monomorphism dominated by pustules. (a) Asymmetrical repartition of lesions on the back of hand showing multiple pustules at the same stages of evolution at the same level of progression; pustular lesions were strongly tense and surrounded by hyperpigmentation and edema for the most part. (b) Multiple asymmetrical pustules, with high density of lesions in relation to the spaces of the palms; strong tendency to confluence or the grouping of lesions with a few coalescing in the form of pseudobullous lesions on the palms. (c) Multiple pustules isolated at the same stage of evolution on the back of the feet.
in_text_mentions: There were noticeable bullous lesions in the vaginal area (Figure 2), and the lesions were asymmetrically distributed (Figure 3) and thicker on the extremities (palms and soles) than on the trunk. Significant painful edema of the labia majora and tense and occasionally confluent pustules were linked to the vaginal lesions (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: On admission, the patient was febrile (38.5°C) but hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed oral and genital ulcers, a maculopapular rash over the trunk, and numerous firm, well-circumscribed, peri-umbilicated pseudopustular lesions on the extremities (Fig. 1). These lesions lacked true purulent material, distinguishing them from typical pustules. Bilateral axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy were palpable and mildly tender.

He also reported dysphagia and the observation of white spots on his tonsils (Fig. 1A). Samples were collected for common STD screening. Two days later, patient #1 had developed several papular skin lesions on the trunk, extremities, and head (Fig. 1B). One lesion on the right wrist was particularly conspicuous (Fig. 1C). Patient #2, a 32-year-old man, presented to his primary care physician on May 19, complaining of fever up to 39.0° Celsius, fatigue, and cough. Two days later, he developed inguinal lymphadenopathy, anal pain, and multiple vesicular skin lesions on the entire trunk (Fig. 1D). He reported having had repeated unprotected homosexual intercourse between May 1 and 17, 2022.

panels.rationale: Real clinical photograph of a 25-year-old hospitalized male (dark skin visible on the legs) with red-arrow-annotated pustular lesions in the perianal region and scattered pustules on the lower extremities. The caption explicitly describes perianal/rectal pustular nodules with surrounding inflammation, and the in-text describes the evolution from presumed HSV to a diffuse vesiculopustular eruption with painful perianal lesions in a case titled 'Severe Anorectal Mpox'. The discrete, raised pustular morphology (rather than flat moist condylomata or a chancre) supports mpox over syphilis for this figure, and the anogenital-plus-extremity pustular eruption is a classic mpox presentation. Red arrows are image annotations. No ethnicity is stated.

in_text_mentions: In June 2024, a 25-year-old male with no known past medical history presented to a tertiary hospital in Florida with rectal bleeding, rectal pain, and newly developed anal lesions of two days’ duration. He was initially diagnosed with herpes simplex virus and discharged with acyclovir. However, five days later, he returned to the emergency department due to worsening symptoms, including the development of diffuse vesicular lesions across his body and painful verrucous lesions surrounding the anus (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: For patient A, mpox suspicion was high upon presentation due to his whole-body rash. However, in the case of patient B, his hand lesion was the first potential hint to mpox, which was not confirmed until 5 days after initial presentation (after discharge). Key characteristics of the mpox rash to watch out for include isolated or disseminated lesions (Figure 4) that are well-circumscribed, firm or rubbery, umbilicated, and painful with progression to pruritis during the healing phase. 9 These lesions may first present on the hands before becoming apparent elsewhere on the patient.

in_text_mentions: oviral therapy (bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide), hemorrhoids, and a recently diagnosed monkeypox virus infection, presented to the hospital with hematochezia. The patient has no history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diverticulosis, colonic polyps, or any prior gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient was tested for the monkeypox virus two weeks prior to this admission after developing painful anal lesions (Figure 1). The PCR test of anal and rectal swabs for monkeypox virus (MPXV) was positive, and he was started on oral tecovirimat (TPOXX) 600 mg twice daily for 14 days.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical manifestations of severe mpox in a patient with advanced HIV-1. Sequential images showing dermatological and mucocutaneous manifestations of severe mpox in a 30-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 55 cells/μL). Early lesions on the hand and arm display classic umbilicated pustules and crusted nodules (A). Involvement of the lower limb includes papulopustular and crusted eruptions (B). Facial and scalp lesions are accompanied by peri-auricular secondary bacterial infection (C). Extensive anogenital disease features a necrotic penile ulcer, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and disseminated lesions over the groin and limbs (D). Widespread trunk eruptions at different stages of development highlight the severity and systemic spread of cutaneous disease (E)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient clinical photograph of the PCR-confirmed mpox index lesion (day 4, vesicle on the pricked finger of a physician after occupational needlestick injury from a pustule); shows an early umbilicated vesicle consistent with mpox. Disease attribution is unambiguous (article title, PCR confirmation). Skin appears light; patient is an adult male physician; no ethnicity stated. B: Real patient clinical photograph of the same PCR-confirmed mpox index lesion on day 6, now a deep-seated pustule with surrounding erythema and swelling. Classic mpox pustular stage. Disease attribution unambiguous. Skin tone light; adult male physician; ethnicity not stated (Portugal is country, not ethnicity). C: Real patient clinical photograph of the index lesion on day 18 of illness, described as necrotic ("The index lesion became necrotic (Figure 1, panel C)"). in_text_mentions: Four days later, a vesicle appeared on the pricked finger (Figure 1, panel A), and monkeypox virus (MPXV) was identified in its fluid by PCR, showing a cycle threshold (Ct) of 28. The HCW was sent on sick leave, with indication for the institution of contact and droplet isolation measures at home.

On the sixth day of illness, fever (temperature 38.4°C), chills, and malaise developed and lasted for ≈48 hours. The finger lesion became pustular and painful and showed surrounding erythema and swelling (Figure 1, panel B). A tender, indurated, erythematous and well-delimited linear streak from the left finger to the armpit appeared on the seventh day (Figure 2, panel A), without regional adenopathy. MPXV PCR was repeated in samples from the oropharynx and blood; again, results were negative.

By the 18th day of illness, all skin lesions, except the one on the left index finger, had evolved through the pustular stage into crust. The index lesion became necrotic (Figure 1, panel C) and was debrided on the 24th day of illness, showing a necrotic scab that had a diameter of 0.5 cm underneath the devitalized tissue (Figure 1, panel D). An MPXV PCR result was still positive in the crust and showed a Ct of 23, but viral culture was negative.

in_text_mentions: mal scarring with vascular proliferation and mixed inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and rare neutrophils. No cytoplasmic inclusion bodies were observed. We conducted an immunohistochemistry assay by using a MPXV polyclonal rabbit antibody and orthopoxviral antigens were identified in the stromal mononuclear cells (Figure 2 panels A, B). The patient had a dense cataract in the same eye (previously obscured by the corneal opacity) and underwent cataract surgery 4 months after the corneal transplant; results of orthopoxvirus PCR of the aspirated lens material were negative.

in_text_mentions: le with a history of poorly controlled HIV/AIDS (not on antiretroviral therapy) and recently treated syphilis presented with intermittent fevers and a 9-day history of a worsening rash. The rash began on the face and perianal area and then spread to the extremities, chest, trunk, and back. Examination revealed diffuse vesicles, pustules, crusted ulcerated papules with serosanguinous drainage, and excoriations (Fig 1). The palms and soles were spared. panels.figure_caption: (a) Presence of scars and necrotic ulcers on the face as well as the involvement of the nasal and buccal mucosa with cheilitis. (b) Involvement of the first, third, and fourth toes of the right foot with edema and color changes, as well as the presence of purulent discharge and necrotic ulcers. (c, d, e, f) Disseminated necrotic ulcers in the face, thorax, anterior abdomen, and palms with involvement of the perianal region as well as the rectal mucosa and umbilicated papules around the necrotic ulcers. (g) Erythematous plaque with color changes and edema.
in_text_mentions: t presented odynophagia, oral intolerance, diarrhea, and weight loss and said that before the first cutaneous lesions, he had anal intercourse, after which, he started experiencing fever (39.0°C) and a perianal abscess, which was treated with oral antibiotics and drainage. Subsequently, skin lesions appeared, characterized by itchy umbilicated vesicles less than 5mm in diameter, beginning on the face but spreading to the entire body, including the palms and soles, with progression to pustules, scabs, and necrotic ulcers, reaching more than 350 in number by the time of his admission (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real-patient clinical photograph from a laboratory-confirmed Mpox case; caption explicitly states the images depict Mpox lesions in pustular stage. Umbilicated pustules on the hand dorsum are the textbook cutaneous presentation of mpox. The prior triage's 'other disease' label is superseded by the panel-specific caption evidence attributing the lesions to Mpox, which is a configured target disease. B: Real-patient clinical photograph; caption explicitly attributes the palmar pustules to Mpox and calls firm pearly palmar pustules a recognised feature of Mpox. Palmar involvement is a classic, well-recognized mpox cutaneous manifestation. C: Real-patient clinical photograph from the same laboratory-confirmed Mpox case; caption attributes the scattered trunk and abdominal lesions to Mpox in pustular and crusting stages. The caption describes a polymorphic appearance characteristic of the current outbreak phenotype, i.e., mixed-stage lesions,...

Panel A: dorsum of the hand with umbilicated pustular lesions; Panel B: palmar surface with firm pearly pustules, a recognised feature of Mpox; Panel C: trunk and lower abdomen showing scattered lesions in pustular and crusting stages, illustrating the polymorphic appearance characteristic of the current outbreak phenotype. All images were captured on the same day of illness (hospital day 9).

in_text_mentions: her differentials, such as herpes simplex since lesional fluid herpes simplex virus1/2 polymerase chain reaction was negative. Interestingly, the Tzanck smear demonstrated multinucleated giant cells (Fig 2). Typically, multinucleated giant cells are not as frequently observed in Tzanck smears of mpox lesions in comparison to herpetic lesions. This case demonstrates that bedside diagnostic tools such as Tzanck smear are important yet may also confound the diagnosis given the presence of multinucleated giant cells in herpes zoster or herpes simplex lesions. in_text_mentions: that same day, his symptoms progressed to fever, muscle aches, sore throat, fatigue, and rash, which primarily affected his genitalia, trunk, extremities, and face. His wife picked him up from Suvarnabhumi Airport (Thailand); they had dinner together in Bangkok before checking into a hotel. On August 15, he visited a private hospital and was admitted. On examination, he had multiple discrete erythematous maculopapular lesions and a few vesicular lesions distributed across his face, trunk, and extremities and had some necrotic papules with overlying scabs on his penis and right thigh (Figure).

plate_findings.evidence: Epidermal necrosis, reticular necrosis, and vesiculation; diffuse mixed superficial dermal infiltrate in the epidermis/dermis on H&E punch biopsy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Human mpox punch biopsy from an abdominal pustule; low-power H&E shows orthopox-type epidermal necrosis/reticular degeneration with vesiculation and superficial mixed dermal infiltrate, consistent with mpox. B: Human mpox skin biopsy at intermediate magnification; histologic orthopox viral cytopathic changes, including dyskeratosis, neutrophil exocytosis and Guarnieri-type inclusions, support mpox. C: Human mpox skin biopsy at high magnification; intracytoplasmic Guarnieri-body inclusions and surrounding epidermal viral cytopathic changes are diagnostic-consistent with mpox.
panels.attribution_text: Costello et al. Imported Monkeypox from International Traveler, Maryland, USA, 2021.. Emerging infectious diseases 2022. doi:10.3201/eid2805.220292. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Imported monkeypox from international traveler, Maryland, USA, 2021. A) Epidermal necrosis, reticular necrosis, and vesiculation. In the dermis, a diffuse mixed superficial dermal infiltrate was observed. B, C) Higher magnification views showing dyskeratotic keratinocytes, neutrophil exocytosis, and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies consistent with Guarnieri bodies in the epidermis. Hematoxylin and eosin stain; original magnification ×4 in panel A, ×20 in panel B, and ×40 in panel C.
in_text_mentions: We obtained a 4-mm punch biopsy specimen from an intact pustule on the abdomen of the patient. This specimen showed epidermal necrosis, reticular degeneration, and vesiculation by staining with hematoxylin and eosin. We found dyskeratotic keratinocytes, neutrophil exocytosis, and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies consistent with Guarnieri bodies in the epidermis. We also detected a diffuse, mixed, superficial dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and occasional eosinophils (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: All lesions were confirmed to be positive for mpox viral DNA, and she was sent to the Infectious Disease Isolation Centre of the hospital, where she was monitored for two more days before being discharged home for isolation. The biopsy results showed multiple multinucleated keratinocytes and focal to full-thickness epidermal necrosis interspersed with extensive dermal inflammatory cells. Few keratinocytes exhibited cytoplasmic filling with eosinophils, with a “ground glass” appearance consistent with viral infection (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: A 21-year-old male flight attendant arrived from Spain at the end of June 2022. He had a history of depression, bronchial asthma, and atopic dermatitis, for which he had been receiving amitriptyline 10mg and sertraline 100mg orally and dupilumab 300mg subcutaneously every two weeks for more than two years, but he never required short- or long-term steroid therapy. He presented initially on July 19, 2022, with a four-day history of very few blistering skin lesions on his face and palms of the hands (Figures 1-2). His monkeypox polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test came back positive (Table 1).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a patient's genital region showing pustular and vesicular lesions (deep-seated, some umbilicated-appearing) on the penile shaft, inner thighs, and hand, indicated by red arrows. The prior caption triage attributes these lesions to mpox, and the article is primarily about severe anorectal mpox. Pustular/vesicular lesions are the hallmark of mpox, not syphilis (which typically presents with chancre or papulosquamous eruptions), so attribution is to mpox with high confidence.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a PCR-confirmed mpox patient showing peri-oral manifestations: an erythematous vesicular plaque on the chin and an oval lower-lip mucosal ulcer with a white peripheral border and central erosion. The article title, in-text prodrome (fever, headache, malaise) with cervical lymphadenopathy, and prior caption triage all support mpox; the failed aciclovir trial excludes the initial suspected herpetic diagnosis. No panel-level annotations, no third-party content.

Scab-like lesions at the gluteal level; most lesions were crusted and painless on the fourteenth day

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient clinical photograph from a confirmed mpox case report, showing a neck lesion at day 14 with a scab/crusted appearance; article title attributes the case to mpox. B: Real patient clinical photograph from a confirmed mpox case report, showing a crusted/scabbed lesion on the left costal grid at day 14. C: Real patient clinical photograph from a confirmed mpox case report, showing multiple scab-like/crusted lesions at the gluteal level, supporting anogenital-region mpox involvement with regional stage uniformity. D: Real patient clinical photograph from a confirmed mpox case report, showing a scabbed/crusted lesion at the sartorius muscle level at day 14.

in_text_mentions: e seventh day: a pustule on the left lateral region of the neck and an erythematous papule on the left costal grill. On the eleventh day, all the lesions in the gluteal region and neck were erythematous-pustular, and some pustules were umbilicated. In addition, the patient mentioned that the lesions in the gluteal region were painful (Figure 2). Most lesions were crusted and painless on the fourteenth day. A papule appeared near the gluteal cleft (Figure 3). On the eighteenth day, several crusts fell off. On the twenty-first day all the scabs fell off and the patient was discharged (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: The liquid contained in the cutaneous vesicles was collected on July 15, 2022, for RT-PCR, which was positive for monkeypox virus. The number of lesions progressively increased from the onset of the first lesion until July 25, 2022, making it a period of approximately two and a half weeks (Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4). The many lesions in the oral cavity caused pharyngitis, limiting oral intake (Figure 5). Therefore, the patient required a nasoenteric tube for feeding.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a hospitalized patient's torso and arm showing annular, raised, pustular (~1 cm) lesions on the abdomen and medial forearm, marked by red arrows. The caption, in-text description of synchronous pustular lesions across torso/extremities, and the mpox-focused article title support attribution to mpox rather than the co-diagnosed syphilis, whose rash is typically papulosquamous. The pustules appear deep-seated and umbilicated, a classic mpox presentation.

in_text_mentions: On clinical examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Physical findings included left inguinal and right axillary lymphadenopathy. Skin lesions were observed across the extremities, lips, face, torso, genitals, and perianal region (Figures 2-5). These lesions were annular, raised, and pustular in appearance, measuring approximately 1 cm in diameter. Notably, the perianal area exhibited extensive verrucous changes and ulcerations (Figure 6).

in_text_mentions: A 21-year-old male flight attendant arrived from Spain at the end of June 2022. He had a history of depression, bronchial asthma, and atopic dermatitis, for which he had been receiving amitriptyline 10mg and sertraline 100mg orally and dupilumab 300mg subcutaneously every two weeks for more than two years, but he never required short- or long-term steroid therapy. He presented initially on July 19, 2022, with a four-day history of very few blistering skin lesions on his face and palms of the hands (Figures 1-2). His monkeypox polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test came back positive (Table 1).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph from an mpox gynecological case report showing pustular lesions on the vulva/labia majora and minora and clitoris, consistent with anogenital mpox. The in-text describes ruptured pustular rashes with raised edges, supporting deep-seated pustules. The mixed pustular and maculopapular morphology argues against regional stage uniformity, so that finding is not applied. No ethnicity or age is stated for this figure.
panels.attribution_text: Abrefa Safo and Sackey. Mpox in a Gynecological Setting: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.92052. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Pustular lesions on both labia majora and minora and the clitoris
in_text_mentions: Status localis examination showed an edematous vulva with bilateral hyperemic labia majora and minora, which were tender on palpation (Figure 1). There were multiple ruptured pustular rashes interspersed with maculopapular forms of about 0.5 cm x 0.5 cm with raised edges (Figure 2). Noted on the vulval skin were excoriations and a creamy, non-offensive discharge. She had a smooth but hyperemic vaginal wall and cervix with no mass felt. No adnexal mass was felt, but she had mild adnexal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness.

in_text_mentions: 24/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He had extensive lymphadenopathy involving the inguinal and cervical regions. Dermatological findings included multiple papules, nodules and vesicles with central necrosis involving the whole body with facial swelling. Similar tense blisters were noted on palms and soles. Herpetic erosion and secondary crusting were noted on the face as per Figure 1. Our differential diagnosis included: Mpox with secondary infection, secondary syphilis, a deep fungal infection, varicella zoster (chickenpox) and disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: H&E low-power (20X) histology of a skin punch biopsy from a PCR-confirmed mpox patient (severe mpox case), showing epidermal ulceration and intense inflammation of the ulcer base and underlying dermis, consistent with mpox viral dermatosis; human patient histopathology, not third-party. b: H&E low-power (100X) histology of the same mpox skin biopsy showing the ulcer base and intact inflamed epidermis at the ulcer shoulder; human patient histopathology from a PCR-confirmed mpox case. c: H&E high-power (400X) histology showing orthopox viral cytopathy within epidermal squamous cells adjacent to the ulcer in a PCR-confirmed mpox skin biopsy; the hallmark histological feature of mpox. d: H&E high-power (1000X) histology showing orthopox viral cytopathy within epidermal squamous cells adjacent to the ulcer in a PCR-confirmed mpox skin biopsy; highest-magnification confirmation of the diagnostic viral cytopathic effect.

panels.figure_caption: Histological evaluation of skin biopsy specimen. Image a: H&E (hematoxylin and eosin–stained histology slides) low power (20X) showing epidermal ulceration and intense inflammation of the ulcer base (arrow) and within the underlying dermis (arrowhead). Image b: H&E low power (100X) showing the ulcer base and intact, inflamed epidermis at the shoulder of the ulcer. Image c: H&E high power (400X) showing a viral cytopathy within epidermal squamous (arrow) adjacent to the ulcer. Image d: H&E high power (1000X) showing a viral cytopathy within epidermal squamous (arrow) adjacent to the ulcer. National Health Laboratory Service laboratory at Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital, 2025.
in_text_mentions: Mpox diagnosis confirmed by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) from lesion swab. A skin punch biopsy on admission had features of a pustule, suggestive of a viral dermatosis. No fungal elements were identified on histological examination, and multinucleated giant cells or ballooning degeneration – features typically associated with varicella or herpes simplex virus infection were not present, making these diagnoses unlikely. The appearances were consistent with mpox as confirmed by PCR. Immunochemistry testing of both HSV and Treponema pallidum was negative (as per Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: On genital examination, the patient had extensive swelling and ulceration of the penile shaft, glans, scrotum, and pubic region, with clear evidence of superimposed infection and necrosis ( Fig. 1 ). And physical examination revealed extensive penile and scrotal edema accompanied by necrosis, multiple vesicular and ulcerative skin lesions scattered across the entire body, and palpable bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy ( Fig. 2 ). Pelvic computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an 8-mm fluid collection along the ventral aspect of the penile shaft, suggesting a penile abscess ( Fig. 3 ).

This was supported by experts in paediatric infectious diseases in Denmark, who received photos and a written file by e-mail. This was due to logistic challenges as well as fear among healthcare workers of handling contagious specimens and because of reluctancy from the project leader to carry out any more tests (see Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Real patient clinical photograph showing papular and vesicular lesions in the anal and perineal region, directly matching the caption and in-text description of the mpox patient's lesions with highest density in the perineal and anal region. Raised umbilicated-appearing papulopustules are visible on dark skin. b: Real patient clinical photograph of the posterior trunk, glutes, and arms showing scattered small papules/pustules consistent with the caption description of singular papules, vesiculae or pustules on glutes and arms in a monkeypox patient.
panels.attribution_text: Fischer et al. Monkeypox in a Patient with Controlled HIV Infection Initially Presenting with Fever, Painful Pharyngitis, and Tonsillitis.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2022. doi:10.3390/medicina58101409. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Papular and vesicular skin lesions affecting the anal and perineal region. (b) Singular papules, vesiculae or pustules on glutes and arms.
in_text_mentions: Upon physical exam, the patient presented with stable vital parameters and was non-febrile. Lymphadenopathy could not be detected. Papulovesicular skin lesions could be found all over the body, with the highest density in the perineal and anal region (Figure 1a). Other papules affected the lower and upper extremities (Figure 1b) and the tip of the tongue (Figure 2). A homogenous, plane and markedly red enanthema were present in the pharyngeal region. Ulcers or vesiculae were absent in the pharynx. The left palatine tonsil appeared ulcerous and swollen.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a hospitalized patient (IV line, wristband) with red arrows marking discrete papulopustular lesions on the forearms/wrists and thighs; the palms are shown and visibly spared. The article is focused on mpox (severe anorectal mpox with HIV and syphilis co-infection), and the prior caption triage attributes these extremity lesions to mpox (route keep). Scattered papulopustular lesions on the extremities are a classic mpox cutaneous presentation; the explicit palmar/finger sparing argues against a palmar syphilid, supporting mpox attribution despite the syphilis co-infection. No ethnicity or age is stated in the caption or text, so those remain unknown; skin tone is judged dark from the well-lit thighs and forearms.

in_text_mentions: On clinical examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Physical findings included left inguinal and right axillary lymphadenopathy. Skin lesions were observed across the extremities, lips, face, torso, genitals, and perianal region (Figures 2-5). These lesions were annular, raised, and pustular in appearance, measuring approximately 1 cm in diameter. Notably, the perianal area exhibited extensive verrucous changes and ulcerations (Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real clinical photo from the PCR-confirmed mpox case 2 (MSM). Shows a classic deep-seated umbilicated pustule with crust on the hair-bearing anogenital/perianal region; disease attribution is certain (positive MPCR) and morphology is textbook mpox. No diagram/control/other-disease content. B: Real clinical photo of an umbilicated pustule on the finger/hand in the PCR-confirmed mpox case; palmar/digital pustules are a classic mpox manifestation. Disease attribution certain; finding clear. C: Real clinical photo of a small erythematous papule/pustule with a central punctum/umbilication on a hairy extremity in the PCR-confirmed mpox case. Disease attribution is certain, but the lesion is small so deep-seated umbilication is less conspicuous than in panels A/B, giving slightly lower finding confidence.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph from a monkeypox case report; caption explicitly identifies the lesion as an MPXV (mpox) rash, an ulcerated lesion of 4 mm. The image shows dark-skinned body skin (trunk) with a small round ulcerated lesion with central umbilication/crusting, consistent with an mpox vesiculopustule in its ulcerative stage, mapped to the vocabulary term for deep-seated umbilicated pustules; the ulceration itself is added as a proposed finding. No subtype, age, or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text mentions, so these are left null/unknown. Attribution to mpox is strong (caption + disease-focused title), and prior caption triage kept this as a real patient clinical photo.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E skin punch biopsy scanning view shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis in a confirmed mpox case; caption/in-text link the biopsy to a viral infection. B: Higher-power H&E shows keratinocyte changes with arrow, and in-text describes orthopox-like viral cytopathic keratinocyte nuclei in the skin biopsy of a confirmed mpox patient. C: H&E panel shows the mixed inflammatory infiltrate described in the skin biopsy from a confirmed mpox case; arrow highlights inflammatory cells. D: H&E panel shows the plasma-cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate from the mpox skin biopsy; arrows highlight plasma cells in the dermal infiltrate.

in_text_mentions: The patient was also referred to the Dermatology service which performed skin punch biopsy. The skin punch biopsy results were consistent with the picture of a viral infection (Figure 3). The epidermis revealed scale crusts and ulceration. Some of the keratinocytes in the epidermis and the upper dermis were large with convoluted steel-gray nuclei and the dermis revealed red blood cell extravasation and a moderately dense, perivascular and interstitial inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a human patient's genital region showing mpox-associated genital necrosis at presentation, consistent with the article title (Monkeypox-Associated Genital Necrosis) and in-text description of extensive swelling, ulceration, and necrosis of the penile shaft, glans, scrotum, and pubic region. Dark necrotic/eschar-like change is visible on the glans with surrounding edema. Anogenital lesion finding is supported by vocabulary; necrosis/edema details are proposed as they are absent from the vocabulary. B: Second clinical photograph of the same patient's anogenital region showing marked scrotal and penile edema with erythema, manipulated by a gloved examiner's hand. Caption and in-text describe mpox-associated genital necrosis with edema, ulceration, and superimposed infection involving the scrotum. Disease attribution to mpox is direct from the article title and presentation context; anogenital lesion finding is in the...

panels.figure_caption: Extensive genital necrosis at presentation. Clinical photograph showing marked edema and ulceration involving the penile shaft, glans, scrotum, and pubic region, with areas of superimposed infection and necrosis.
in_text_mentions: On genital examination, the patient had extensive swelling and ulceration of the penile shaft, glans, scrotum, and pubic region, with clear evidence of superimposed infection and necrosis ( Fig. 1 ). And physical examination revealed extensive penile and scrotal edema accompanied by necrosis, multiple vesicular and ulcerative skin lesions scattered across the entire body, and palpable bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy ( Fig. 2 ). Pelvic computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an 8-mm fluid collection along the ventral aspect of the penile shaft, suggesting a penile abscess ( Fig. 3 ).

in_text_mentions: Clinical dermatological findings are displayed on Fig. 1. Skin biopsies (Fig. 2) showed a partially necrotic epithelium with scale, crust, and mounds of parakeratosis. Marked acanthosis, vacuolated keratinocytes with bluish-gray cytoplasm and enforcement of nucleus membrane, and some multinucleated giant cells were observed as distinctive of Mpox infection. A lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial mucosa accompanied these changes. Periodic acid Schiff (PAS), Ziel-Nielsen (ZN), Fite Faraco, and Gram stains were negative.

in_text_mentions: In the emergency department, his vitals were T-98.9F, HR-94 bpm, BP-135/89 mmHg, RR-18, O2 sat-96% on room air. Upon review of systems, the patient endorsed watery diarrhea for one month. Physical examination exhibited newly developing monkeypox lesions along the left forearm and in the mouth superimposed on oral thrush (Fig. 1A and B) as well as confluence and necrosis of week-old lesions along the left knee and buttocks/anal region extending to the scrotum (Fig. 1C and D).

Our patient, who presented with several diarrheal illnesses, likely had an inability to properly absorb dietary fat. It is also possible that our patient had some degree of HIV enteropathy, which is a direct HIV-mediated and indirect immune-mediated injury to the GI tract mucosa [10]. Beyond the physiological barriers to adequate absorption of oral tecovirimat, our patient also had painful MPXV lesions of the tongue along with severe oral candida that reduced his ability to tolerate any oral intake (Fig. 1B).

in_text_mentions: On admission, the pustular lesions had begun to evolve but remained distributed across the same regions noted in the emergency department (Figures 2, 3). Perianal erythema and tenderness were again present, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable. Upon further discussion, the patient disclosed that he had recently traveled to Minnesota, where he engaged in unprotected receptive anal and oral intercourse with a male partner approximately one week before the onset of symptoms. He denied genital ulcers, urethral discharge, or oral lesions.

panels.rationale: Real clinical photograph of the mpox patient taken before her first hospital visit. It visibly shows the primary mpox skin lesion on the chin (a 4 cm inflamed crusted/umbilicated nodule) together with red-arrow-highlighted swollen regional lymph nodes, matching the in-text description and the mpox article context. The facial lesion is not anogenital, oral mucosal, palmar or plantar, and no mpox subtype is stated, so subtype is null. Lymphadenopathy is clearly present but absent from the allowed vocabulary, hence recorded as a proposed finding. The visible adequately lit skin is light (Fitzpatrick I-II); ethnicity is not stated.

in_text_mentions: resented with a 4 cm inflamed nodule on her chin, accompanied by fever, swollen lymph nodes, body aches, and general malaise. The lesion was initially misdiagnosed as a localized skin infection (Fig. 1). The patient reported close physical contact, including “cuddling,” with a confirmed MPOX case at a birthday party in Berlin, although no sexual contact occurred. Despite surgical drainage and antibiotic treatment, the lesion did not resolve, leading the patient to seek care in our outpatient clinic (Fig. 2). A second, smallpox-like lesion on her right forearm raised suspicion of MPOX (Fig. 3).

in_text_mentions: On examination, the patient had 4 ulcerated penile lesions that had consolidated into a 3-cm patch present on the foreskin, 2 days after constitutional symptoms developed (Figure, panel A). The lesions were nontender to palpation, and no discharge was present. A tender 3-cm right inguinal lymph node was present. A vaccination scar was noted on his right deltoid, but the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Clinically the patient did well, only requiring supportive care with oral acetaminophen for constitutional symptoms, which resolved 10 days after symptom onset. The rash continued to evolve, coalesced, and developed a pustular appearance 6 days after onset of constitutional symptoms (Figure, panel B). The lesion ulcerated on day 16 (Figure, panel C), and ultimately dissipated without residual scarring (Figure, panel D).

panels.rationale: Single-panel real-patient clinical photograph of the oropharynx. The caption states imaging followed laboratory confirmation of Mpox and describes scattered ulcerative and vesiculopustular lesions on the soft palate, tonsillar pillars, and tongue base plus a small crusted lesion on the upper cutaneous lip — vesiculopustular lesions characteristic of mpox, not of acute tonsillitis/pharyngitis (which would show erythema, exudate, palatal petechiae, or uvular edema). Although the article title frames the case as Mpox presenting like acute tonsillitis, the panel-specific caption evidence attributes the lesions to Mpox, so the panel is tagged mpox and the tonsillitis mimicry is not tagged. The article title explicitly labels the presentation atypical, supporting typicality=atypical. Visible facial and lip skin is adequately lit and appears medium brown (≈ Fitzpatrick III–IV); no ethnicity or age is stated in the caption or in-text mentions. No overlay annotations are present.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real-patient contrast-enhanced axial CT showing rectal wall thickening and enhancement (yellow arrow) in a case whose proctitis is attributed to mpox by the article title ('Atypical Mpox Presentation With Proctitis') and in-text discussion; the anogenital mucosal (rectal) involvement falls under the anogenital mpox manifestation spectrum. Not a diagram, not third-party (prior triage: keep), and the annotation arrows mark the rectal wall abnormality. B: Real-patient contrast-enhanced sagittal CT showing circumferential rectal wall thickening with mucosal enhancement (yellow arrow), the same mpox-associated proctitis manifestation described in the article title and in-text. Real diagnostic radiology image of untreated disease, not third-party, annotated with arrows pointing to the abnormal rectal wall.
panels.attribution_text: López Martínez et al. Atypical Mpox Presentation With Proctitis in a Puerto Rican Patient: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.99869. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis: (A) Axial view showing noticeable thickening and enhancement of the rectal wall (arrow). (B) Sagittal view demonstrating circumferential thickening and mucosal enhancement of the rectal wall (arrow), consistent with inflammatory changes.
in_text_mentions: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast, which revealed circumferential rectal wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and fat stranding, compatible with inflammatory proctitis (Figure 1). Admission laboratory studies were notable for leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers, while renal function remained within normal limits (Table 1). The elevated CRP and leukocytosis further supported an active inflammatory process and aligned with the patient’s worsening anorectal symptoms. Initial management included Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours and Metronidazole 500 mg IV e

Some developed limited anogenital lesions with few or no systemic symptoms [1,3,7]. Mitjà and colleagues observed that men who engage in anal-receptive intercourse were more likely to present with proctitis [1], which aligns with our patient’s CT findings and symptom profile (Figure 1). Because localized lesions, rectal discomfort, and mild systemic symptoms closely resemble conditions such as HSV, syphilis, gonorrhea, or LGV, Mpox is often misdiagnosed in low-incidence regions, which may contribute to diagnostic delays, explaining why our patient was initially treated for bacterial proctitis.

At this stage, septic peritonsillar abscess was suspected due to the clinical presentation of significant tonsillar swelling and localized pain.
